brief.headline: Push for a second source and 45-day payment terms — they're a trader in grey financial health, taking 105 days to pay their own suppliers while we pay in 30.

priceAsk.summary: Hold price steady; ask them to justify any increase against the open-market asking price for a 28 mm PP cap of ₹0.55–1.20/pc (typical ₹0.85–0.95/pc).
priceAsk.target: No price increase; any quote should fall in the ₹0.55–1.20/pc band, ideally ₹0.65–0.80/pc at higher volume.
priceAsk.basis: Market data shows PP caps at ₹0.55–1.20/pc asking price, with modest room to ₹0.65–0.80/pc at scale. They are a 100% trader — their price includes a reseller margin, so we should benchmark against a maker's price and push them toward the lower end of that band.

paymentTermAsk.summary: Move from 30 days to 45 days after receipt — a 15-day stretch that gives us breathing room and mirrors how they treat their own suppliers.
paymentTermAsk.cashImpact: Stretching payment by 15 days frees up ₹2.68 L in cash for us.

brief.financialLeverage: They keep only 2.8% of every ₹100 they sell as profit, and their overall money-health score is just 2/10 — weak, with a grey-zone distress signal (Altman Z 1.58) and pending legal cases. Yet they already take 105 days to pay their own suppliers (far longer than the 57d similar firms take), so they clearly manage tight cash by pushing terms downstream. We are 1.19% of their ₹54.69 Cr in sales — a meaningful customer — so we have the weight to ask for longer terms (to 45 days) and to insist they hold price. But their fragility means the main play is lining up a robust second source, not squeezing them so hard they fail and disrupt our supply.

evidence.point: They are a 100% trader — no manufacturing; their price includes a reseller margin we should negotiate away by benchmarking to a maker.
Market asking price for a 28 mm PP cap is ₹0.55–1.20/pc, typically ₹0.85–0.95/pc, with room to ₹0.65–0.80/pc at higher volume — a concrete benchmark for any quote they give us.

evidence.point: They take 105 days to pay their own suppliers, while similar firms pay in 57 days — so asking for 45-day terms (15 days longer than our current 30) is entirely fair.
Their money-health score is weak at 2/10, and they sit in the grey distress zone (Altman Z 1.58) with pending legal cases — real supply risk.

evidence.point: We spend ₹65.27 L a year with them — 1.19% of their ₹54.69 Cr revenue — enough clout to ask for better terms and to demand they hold price.
They keep only 2.8% profit on every sale, so there's little room for a big price cut without hurting them (and our supply); focus the win on payment terms and a second source instead.

alternates.name: Manjushree Technopack Ltd
alternates.why: India's largest rigid-plastic packaging converter (₹2569.83 Cr revenue, health B 65/100) — pharma bottles, caps, preforms — the strongest second-source candidate to qualify now.

alternates.name: Mold-Tek Packaging Ltd
alternates.why: Listed rigid-plastic leader (₹1010.97 Cr revenue, health B 73/100) for pails, containers, pharma — a robust, profitable alternate for bottles and closures.

risks: Their weak financial health (2/10 score, grey distress zone, legal cases) and 100% traded model mean supply could falter — do not load more volume onto them until a second source is qualified and active.

They have almost no profit cushion (2.8%) and sit in financial grey zone — pushing price too hard risks tipping them over; the smart play is payment terms (to 45 days) and a backup supplier, not a steep price cut.

They borrow at rates ranging 8.95–18% (though effective rate is just 0.1%), so offering faster payment (say, 15 days) in exchange for a small price cut is worth exploring — but only after we have an alternate lined up.
No visibility into which maker supplies them (100% traded) — if we can identify and approach that upstream source directly, we cut out their reseller margin entirely and gain supply security.
brief.suggestedOpeningLine: We'd like to talk about moving to 45-day payment terms — since you already take 105 days with your own suppliers — and about holding price steady while we qualify a second source to share the load and protect both of us.
